claim: 3D single-molecule diffusion simulations predicted a ~6000% increase in EB1 arrivals to open, tapered microtubule tip structures relative to closed lattice conformations.
source: our 3D single-molecule diffusion simulations predicted a ~ 6000% increase in EB1 arrivals to open, tapered microtubule tip structures relative to closed lattice conformations.
evidence: The claim is supported by computational simulations described in the manuscript, which constitute data generated by the authors.

claim: The binding of EB1 onto opened, structurally disrupted microtubules was dramatically increased relative to closed, intact microtubules, regardless of hydrolysis state.
source: Using quantitative fluorescence, single-molecule, and electron microscopy experiments, we found that the binding of EB1 onto opened, structurally disrupted microtubules was dramatically increased relative to closed, intact microtubules, regardless of hydrolysis state.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple experimental approaches (fluorescence, single-molecule, and electron microscopy) described in the manuscript.

claim: In cells, the blunting of growing microtubule plus-ends by Vinblastine was correlated with reduced EB1 targeting.
source: Correspondingly, in cells, the blunting of growing microtubule plus-ends by Vinblastine was correlated with reduced EB1 targeting.
evidence: The claim is supported by cellular experiments with Vinblastine treatment described in the manuscript.

claim: Microtubule structural recognition, based on a fundamental diffusion-limited binding model, facilitates the tip tracking of EB1 at growing microtubule ends.
source: Together, our results suggest that microtubule structural recognition, based on a fundamental diffusion-limited binding model, facilitates the tip tracking of EB1 at growing microtubule ends.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the combined experimental and simulation data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Microtubules are long, thin polymers that mechanically contribute to cell morphology, act as a track for molecular motor-based transport within the cell, and serve as a platform for binding of microtubule-associated proteins.
source: Microtubules are long, thin polymers that mechanically contribute to cell morphology, act as a track for molecular motor-based transport within the cell, and serve as a platform for binding of microtubule-associated proteins (Howard and Hyman, 2003; Mitchison and Kirschner, 1984; Ross et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: A microtubule is typically composed of 13 laterally associated protofilaments.
source: Typically, a microtubule is composed of 13 laterally associated protofilaments (Tilney et al., 1973).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior literature and represents established knowledge.

claim: Each tubulin heterodimer contains an exchangeable nucleotide site on the β-tubulin subunit.
source: Each tubulin heterodimer contains an exchangeable nucleotide site on the β-tubulin subunit
evidence: This is established knowledge about tubulin structure.

claim: Individual tubulin heterodimers polymerize onto the plus-end of the microtubule with the β-tubulin subunit bound to a GTP nucleotide.
source: individual tubulin heterodimers polymerize onto the plus-end of the microtubule with the β-tubulin subunit bound to a GTP nucleotide.
evidence: This is established knowledge about microtubule polymerization.

claim: After integration into the microtubule, the β-tubulin-bound nucleotide stochastically undergoes hydrolysis and converts via GDP-Pi to GDP.
source: After integration into the microtubule, the β-tubulin-bound nucleotide then stochastically undergoes hydrolysis and converts via GDP-Pi to GDP.
evidence: This is established knowledge about GTP hydrolysis in microtubules.

claim: GDP-bound tubulin is less stable in the microtubule lattice than GTP-bound tubulin.
source: GDP-bound tubulin is less stable in the microtubule lattice than GTP-bound tubulin
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The microtubule remains intact and continues to grow at its plus-end due to the continued addition of GTP-bound tubulin, which forms a 'GTP cap' at the growing plus-end of the microtubule.
source: but the microtubule remains intact and continues to grow at its plus-end due to the continued addition of GTP-bound tubulin, which forms a 'GTP cap' at the growing plus-end of the microtubule (Desai and Mitchison, 1997; Mitchison and Kirschner, 1984).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the GTP cap model, supported by citations.

claim: Microtubule plus-ends have been observed by cryo-electron microscopy to have open, sheet-like or tapered conformations.
source: In contrast, microtubule plus-ends have been observed by cryo-electron microscopy to have open, sheet-like or tapered conformations, which diverge greatly from a closed tube conformation (Chrétien et al., 1995; Guesdon et al., 2016; Manka and Moores, 2018a).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior cryo-EM studies.

claim: Tapered microtubule tip structures have been supported by quantitative analysis of fluorescence images.
source: These findings have also been supported by quantitative analysis of fluorescence images (Coombes et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Tapered, gently curved tip structure likely plays a role in the binding of Doublecortin and other proteins to microtubule plus-ends.
source: This type of tapered, gently curved tip structure likely plays a role in the binding of Doublecortin and other proteins to microtubule plus-ends (Bechstedt and Brouhard, 2012; Bechstedt et al., 2014); reviewed in Brouhard and Rice (2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature and represents an inference from those studies.

claim: Lattice damage and tubulin turnover can occur on the microtubule lattice itself, leading to irregularities along the length of a dynamic microtubule.
source: Further, it has recently been reported that lattice damage and tubulin turnover can occur on the microtubule lattice itself, leading to irregularities along the length of a dynamic microtubule (Schaedel et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: EB1 is a highly conserved protein that autonomously tracks the growing plus-ends of microtubules.
source: The microtubule tip tracking protein EB1 is a highly conserved protein that autonomously tracks the growing plus-ends of microtubules (Bieling et al., 2007; Dixit et al., 2009; Morrison et al., 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature and represents established knowledge.

claim: At the plus-end, EB1 recruits many other +TIP family proteins that have little to no native affinity for microtubules but that must localize to microtubule plus ends to perform their functions.
source: At the plus-end, EB1 recruits many other +TIP family proteins that have little to no native affinity for microtubules but that must localize to microtubule plus ends to perform their functions (Bieling et al., 2007; Dixit et al., 2009; Lansbergen and Akhmanova, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: High-affinity binding of EB1 to the GTP-cap at growing microtubule plus-ends may contribute to its plus-end localization.
source: High-affinity binding of EB1 to the GTP-cap at growing microtubule plus-ends may contribute to its plus-end localization (Maurer et al., 2011; Zanic et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature and represents a hypothesis from those studies.

claim: The increased affinity of EB1 for GTP tubulin relative to GDP tubulin has been demonstrated through the use of GTP analogs, most commonly GMPCPP and GTP-γ-S.
source: The increased affinity of EB1 for GTP tubulin relative to GDP tubulin has been demonstrated through the use of GTP analogs, most commonly GMPCPP and GTP-γ-S.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: There was an increase in overall EB1 binding to the GTP-analog-bound microtubules as compared to GDP-microtubules.
source: In both cases, there was an increase in overall EB1 binding to the GTP-analog-bound microtubules as compared to GDP-microtubules (Maurer et al., 2011; Zanic et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: At 30 mM KCl, EB1 was often localized to GMPCPP microtubule ends.
source: Interestingly, we observed that, at 30 mM KCl, EB1 was often localized to GMPCPP microtubule ends (Figure 1B, green).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 1B.

claim: An increase in EB1-GFP intensity was observed at the brighter EB1-GFP microtubule end as compared to the center region and the dimmer EB1-GFP end of the microtubule.
source: Similar to our qualitative observations, an increase in EB1-GFP intensity was observed at the brighter EB1-GFP microtubule end as compared to the center region and the dimmer EB1-GFP end of the microtubule (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The red microtubule fluorescence on the right (brighter EB1-GFP) side of the line-scan plot appeared to drop off more slowly to background as compared to the left side of the line-scan plot.
source: Here, the red microtubule fluorescence on the right (brighter EB1-GFP) side of the line-scan plot appeared to drop off more slowly to background as compared to the left side of the line-scan plot (Figure 1C, compare teal vs magenta line lengths).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The microtubule end with a brighter EB1-GFP signal had a larger average tip standard deviation than the opposite, dimmer EB1-GFP signal end, of the microtubule.
source: Importantly, regardless of microtubule length, we found that the microtubule end with a brighter EB1-GFP signal had a larger average tip standard deviation, and thus more tip tapering due to protofilament length variation, than the opposite, dimmer EB1-GFP signal end, of the microtubule (Figure 1D; 2.1 ± 0.3 μm group (mean ± SD): p=0.00017, Z-statistic = 3.79; 2.9 ± 0.2 μm group (mean ± SD): p=0.013, Z-statistic = 2.47; Fit curves in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 1D and supplementary figures.

claim: Tapered and blunt ends were present in the GMPCPP microtubule population.
source: We then used both Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM) and Cryo-Electron Microscopy to verify that tapered and blunt ends were indeed present in the GMPCPP microtubule population (Figure 1E), similar to previous observations (Atherton et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 1E and a citation to prior work.

claim: The average transition point, plus-end, and minus end of the GMPCPP microtubules all showed a significantly higher fraction of EB1-GFP fluorescence than the GMPCPP lattice position.
source: We found that the average transition point (p<<10−5, t-test), plus-end (p<10−8, t-test), and minus end (p=0.0039, t-test) of the GMPCPP microtubules all showed a significantly higher fraction of EB1-GFP fluorescence than the GMPCPP lattice position (Figure 1G; n = 309 microtubules).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 1G.

claim: EB1-GFP intensity was ~2.3 fold (230%) higher at growing microtubule plus-ends as compared to the overall average intensity on the GDP lattice and GMPCPP seeds.
source: We found that, as would be expected, EB1-GFP intensity was ~2.3 fold (230%) higher at growing microtubule plus-ends as compared to the overall average intensity on the GDP lattice and GMPCPP seeds (Figure 1G bottom-left, cyan).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The EB1-GFP fluorescence at the GMPCPP/GDP transition point was 38% higher than the average intensity on the GDP lattice and GMPCPP seeds.
source: However, consistent with our GMPCPP microtubule results, the EB1-GFP fluorescence at the GMPCPP/GDP transition point was 38% higher than the average intensity on the GDP lattice and GMPCPP seeds (Figure 1G bottom-left; p<10−5 vs GDP lattice, p<10−6 vs GMPCPP seeds, n = 134 microtubules).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The average EB1-GFP/tubulin intensity ratio in the disrupted-structure microtubule pool was ~98% higher than the average EB1-GFP/tubulin intensity ratio in the closed microtubule pool for GDP microtubules.
source: Upon quantification, the average EB1-GFP/tubulin intensity ratio in the disrupted-structure microtubule pool was ~98% higher than the average EB1-GFP/tubulin intensity ratio in the closed microtubule pool (Figure 2C, bottom; p<<10−5, t-test).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The average EB1-GFP/tubulin intensity ratio in the disrupted-structure GMPCPP microtubule pool was ~75% higher than the average EB1-GFP/tubulin intensity ratio in the closed microtubules.
source: GMPCPP microtubules from the disrupted-structure pool also showed an increase in the average EB1-GFP/tubulin intensity ratio (Figure 2D, top), which was ~75% higher than the average EB1-GFP/tubulin intensity ratio in the closed microtubules (Figure 2D, bottom; p<<10−5, t-test).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The average EB1-GFP/tubulin intensity ratio was ~50% higher on disrupted-structure GTPγS microtubules as compared to closed GTPγS microtubules.
source: Finally, the average EB1-GFP/tubulin intensity ratio was higher on disrupted-structure GTPγS microtubules as compared to closed GTPγS microtubules, with a quantitative increase of ~50% (Figure 2E; p<<10−5, t-test).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: EB1-gold beads were nearly four-fold more likely to bind at defects or sheets than to a complete microtubule lattice.
source: However, when we normalized the frequency of bead location to the total available microtubule length for each classification, we found that the EB1-gold beads were nearly four-fold more likely to bind at defects or sheets than to a complete microtubule lattice (Figure 2G; p<2.3×10−54, Chi-squared test).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of electron microscopy data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: The mean number of successful arrival events of EB1 onto individual 'disrupted-structure' microtubules was ~33% higher than onto closed 'blunt' microtubules with the same number of tubulin subunits in simulations.
source: We found that the mean number of successful arrival events of EB1 onto individual 'disrupted-structure' microtubules was ~33% higher than onto closed 'blunt' microtubules with the same number of tubulin subunits (Figure 3D; p<<10−5, Binomial test).
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The EB1 molecules had arrived at nearly all of the sites at the microtubule end or along laterally exposed protofilaments, while very few arrived within a complete, closed lattice in simulations.
source: Strikingly, by examining the simulated arrival locations of individual EB1 molecules, we found that the EB1 molecules had arrived at nearly all of the sites at the microtubule end or along laterally exposed protofilaments, while very few arrived within a complete, closed lattice, both for the closed and the 'disrupted-structure' microtubules (Figure 3E, random representative subset of 10,000 simulated EB1 molecules).
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The fraction of EB1 arrivals was ~70 fold higher for 2-tubulin sites with lower steric hindrance as compared to 4-tubulin sites on the closed microtubule lattice in simulations.
source: Strikingly, in this simulation, the fraction of EB1 arrivals was ~70 fold higher for 2-tubulin sites with lower steric hindrance, such as those at protofilament edges (Figure 3H, dark red), as compared to 4-tubulin sites on the closed microtubule lattice (Figure 3H, light red; p<<10−5, Chi-squared test).
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 3H.

claim: For sheet-like regions of microtubules, there were sevenfold more beads associated with sheet edges than with the middle of the sheet.
source: We observed that, for sheet-like regions of microtubules, there were sevenfold more beads associated with sheet edges than with the middle of the sheet (Figure 3I, right; p<<10−5, Chi-squared test).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of electron microscopy data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: The association rate for EB1-GFP was ~45 fold higher for disrupted-structure microtubules as compared to closed microtubules for the GDP microtubule pools.
source: We found that the association rate for EB1-GFP was ~45 fold higher for disrupted-structure microtubules as compared to closed microtubules for the GDP microtubule pools (Figure 3J, center, teal; p<<10−5; Z-test).
evidence: The claim is supported by rapid frame-rate fluorescence microscopy experiments shown in Figure 3J.

claim: For the GMPCPP microtubule pool, there was a ~12 fold increase in the EB1-GFP association rate constant in the disrupted-structure microtubule pool relative to the closed pool.
source: For the GMPCPP microtubule pool, there was a ~ 12 fold increase in the EB1-GFP association rate constant in the disrupted-structure microtubule pool relative to the closed pool (Figure 3J, center, purple; p<10−64; Z-test)
evidence: The claim is supported by rapid frame-rate fluorescence microscopy experiments shown in Figure 3J.

claim: The EB1-GFP association rate constant was ~3.5 fold higher in the disrupted-structure microtubule pool as compared to the closed microtubules for the GTPγS microtubules.
source: Finally, the EB1-GFP association rate constant was ~3.5 fold higher in the disrupted-structure microtubule pool as compared to the closed microtubules for the GTPγS microtubules (Figure 3J, right, brown; p=1.7×10−16; Z-test).
evidence: The claim is supported by rapid frame-rate fluorescence microscopy experiments shown in Figure 3J.

claim: All pools of disrupted-structure microtubules had lower characteristic dwell-times than their respective closed pools.
source: We found that all pools of disrupted-structure microtubules had lower characteristic dwell-times than their respective closed pools (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The mean number of face-binding molecule arrival events for disrupted-structure microtubules was not substantially increased relative to the closed microtubules in simulations.
source: In contrast, we found that when the protein binding site was located on the tubulin heterodimer's outward face, the mean number of face-binding molecule arrival events for disrupted-structure microtubules was not substantially increased relative to the closed microtubules (Figure 4D, blue; p=0.046, Binomial test; 4000 face-binding molecules per simulation, 50 simulations)
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The face-binding protein arrival events were located non-specifically along the lattice, and with no enrichment on edge dimers in simulations.
source: Similarly, the previous observation that simulated, pocket-binding EB1 molecules showed preferential arrivals to edge-proximal tubulin heterodimers (Figure 4E, red) was strikingly altered in the tubulin face-binding simulations: the face-binding protein arrival events were located non-specifically along the lattice, and with no enrichment on edge dimers (Figure 4F, blue; random representative subset of 10,000 simulated EB1 molecules).
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The average Kif5B-GFP/tubulin intensity ratio for the disrupted-structure pool of GDP microtubules was not higher than in the closed microtubules.
source: Quantification of the TIRF images demonstrated that the average Kif5B-GFP/tubulin intensity ratio for the disrupted-structure pool of GDP microtubules was not higher than in the closed microtubules (p=1; one-sided t-test), but rather appeared to be slightly lower than in the closed microtubules (p=2.7×10−7, 2-sided t-test)
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 4G.

claim: EB1-GFP binding appeared to be reduced on GDP+Pi microtubules relative to GDP microtubules, for both closed and disrupted-structure microtubules.
source: Surprisingly, EB1-GFP binding appeared to be reduced on GDP+Pi microtubules relative to GDP microtubules, for both closed and disrupted-structure microtubules (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 5B.

claim: There was a −53% reduction in binding of EB1-GFP to closed GDP+Pi microtubules relative to closed GDP microtubules.
source: By quantifying EB1-GFP binding on each microtubule type using our previously described automated analysis tool (Reid et al., 2017), we found that there was a −53% reduction in binding of EB1-GFP to closed GDP+Pi microtubules relative to closed GDP microtubules (p<<10−5, t-test) (Figure 5C, experimental repeats Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: EB1 binding data was best fit using a cooperative binding curve, which demonstrated a ~2 fold lower affinity of EB1 for the GDP-Pi-Analog relative to the GDP microtubules.
source: As previously described, the EB1 binding data was best fit using a cooperative binding curve (Lopez and Valentine, 2016; Zhu et al., 2009), and so we fit the results in each case to a Hill equation, which demonstrated a ~ 2 fold lower affinity of EB1 for the GDP-Pi-Analog relative to the GDP microtubules (Figure 5E, see Materials and methods; Kd,GDP=1.9x105 nM, nGDP = 2.2; Kd,Analogue=4.2x105 nM, nAnalogue = 2.3).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The microtubule tip standard deviation was significantly reduced with Vinblastine treatments as low as 1 nM.
source: Consistent with our qualitative observations, we found that the microtubule tip standard deviation was significantly reduced with Vinblastine treatments as low as 1 nM (Figure 6C; Control vs 1 nM: p=0.004, Z = 2.89; Control vs 10 nM: p=6×10−5, Z = 4.01)
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Peak EB1-GFP intensity at microtubule ends was reduced with increasing Vinblastine concentrations.
source: Consistent with qualitative observations (Figure 6D, bottom, white arrows), we found that peak EB1-GFP intensity at microtubule ends was reduced with increasing Vinblastine concentrations (Figure 6E, p<<10−5, t-test)
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The binding of EB1-GFP to closed GDP microtubules was similar regardless of Vinblastine concentration.
source: Importantly, and in contrast to the reduced peak intensity of EB1-GFP comets on dynamic microtubules in cells, the binding of EB1-GFP to closed GDP microtubules was similar regardless of Vinblastine concentration (Figure 6G, no significant differences, t-test; experiment repeats, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 6G.

claim: The Kd of Pi for GDP is ~25 mM.
source: It has been previously shown that the Kd of Pi for GDP is ~25 mM (Carlier et al., 1988; Raw et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The depolymerization rate of GDP microtubules is substantially slowed in the presence of 50 mM of inorganic phosphate.
source: Furthermore, the depolymerization rate of GDP microtubules is substantially slowed in the presence of 50 mM of inorganic phosphate, indicating that Pi binds to GDP-tubulin under these conditions (Carlier et al., 1988).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Vinblastine does not alter the hydrolysis rate of GTP-tubulin.
source: While Vinblastine does not alter the hydrolysis rate of GTP-tubulin (Castle et al., 2017), it interferes with tubulin assembly into protofilaments (Gigant et al., 2005)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Vinblastine interferes with tubulin assembly into protofilaments.
source: While Vinblastine does not alter the hydrolysis rate of GTP-tubulin (Castle et al., 2017), it interferes with tubulin assembly into protofilaments (Gigant et al., 2005)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: EB1 recognizes and rapidly binds to the protofilament edges at open, tapered microtubule end structures.
source: Taken together, our results suggest a new model to explain EB1 tip tracking at growing microtubule plus-ends, in which EB1 recognizes and rapidly binds to the protofilament edges at open, tapered microtubule end structures.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined experimental and simulation data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The subsequent addition of new GTP-tubulin subunits may facilitate the maturation of EB1 into a high-affinity binding state on the closed GTP-tubulin lattice.
source: The subsequent addition of new GTP-tubulin subunits may then facilitate the maturation of EB1 into a high-affinity binding state on the closed GTP-tubulin lattice.
evidence: This is a mechanistic hypothesis based on the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Tubulin hydrolysis into a GDP-Pi or GDP state destroys the EB1 binding site, catalyzing its release from the microtubule.
source: Ultimately, tubulin hydrolysis into a GDP-Pi or GDP state destroys the EB1 binding site, catalyzing its release from the microtubule (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: EB1 dwell time distributions on disrupted structure microtubules were best modeled as two exponential distributions.
source: We found that EB1 dwell time distributions on our disrupted structure microtubules were best modeled as two exponential distributions (Fig S2C,D), including one with a short dwell time (~20 ms), which could be associated with edge-bound EB1.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of experimental data.

claim: In 10 µM tubulin, a free tubulin subunit would arrive to the growing end of the microtubule as rapidly as every ~2 ms.
source: In evaluating this dwell time relative to the kinetics of αβ-tubulin association, in 10 µM tubulin it has been estimated that a free tubulin subunit would arrive to the growing end of the microtubule as rapidly as every ~2 ms (Gardner et al., 2011), or as slowly as every ~10 ms (Mickolajczyk et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The on-rate for EB1 binding to the closed microtubule lattice would be extremely low, due to very high steric hindrance and low accessibility.
source: Specifically, our results predict that the on-rate for EB1 binding to the closed microtubule lattice would be extremely low, due to very high steric hindrance and low accessibility.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the simulation results presented in the manuscript.

claim: The EB1 on-rate would be ~70 fold (~6000%) higher at tapered, growing microtubule plus-ends, due to the presence of easily accessible, low steric hindrance sites at exposed protofilament edges.
source: In contrast, we predict that the EB1 on-rate would be ~70 fold (~6000%) higher at tapered, growing microtubule plus-ends, due to the presence of easily accessible, low steric hindrance sites at exposed protofilament edges.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the simulation results presented in the manuscript.

claim: The overall affinity of EB1 may be higher on disrupted structures, regardless of the likely increase in off-rates.
source: However, our results show an increase in steady-state binding to disrupted microtubule structures, regardless of nucleotide state (Figure 2C–E), suggesting that the overall affinity of EB1 may be higher on disrupted structures, regardless of the likely increase in off-rates.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data shown in Figure 2C-E.

claim: The effect of microtubule structure on microtubule-associated protein binding preference is not likely restricted to EB1.
source: The effect of microtubule structure on microtubule-associated protein binding preference is not likely restricted to EB1, as we find that this preference stems from the physical accessibility of microtubule binding sites, and thus may be pertinent to any polymer binding protein.
evidence: This is a generalization and speculation based on the findings for EB1.

claim: Any protein that has its binding site located in the dip between protofilaments or at the crease between stacked subunits could potentially display microtubule structural recognition.
source: Here, any protein that has its binding site located in the dip between protofilaments or at the crease between stacked subunits could potentially display microtubule structural recognition.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the findings for EB1.

claim: The microtubule-associated protein Doublecortin (DCX) has a similar binding site to EB1.
source: For example, the microtubule-associated protein Doublecortin (DCX) has a similar binding site to EB1.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about DCX binding.

claim: DCX has been reported to recognize microtubule curvature.
source: DCX has been reported to recognize microtubule curvature, a configuration that would require an incomplete lattice with exposed protofilament edges to allow for outward protofilament curvature (Bechstedt and Brouhard, 2012; Bechstedt et al., 2014; Fourniol et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Microtubules grown in the presence of CLIP-170 have been associated with the growth of curved oligomers.
source: Similarly, microtubules grown in the presence of CLIP-170 have been associated with the growth of curved oligomers (Arnal et al., 2004)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Microtubule lattice defects may be recognized by CLIP-170 to stimulate microtubule rescue.
source: and it has been shown that microtubule lattice defects may be recognized by CLIP-170 to stimulate microtubule rescue (de Forges et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The tips of growing microtubules within mitotic spindles display a gentle outward curvature of individual protofilaments.
source: Further, a recent electron microscopy study reported that the tips of growing microtubules within mitotic spindles display a gentle outward curvature of individual protofilaments (McIntosh et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Proteins such as TPX2, which binds in part across the faces of α and β tubulin subunits, may be less likely to display structural recognition.
source: In contrast, proteins such as TPX2, which binds in part across the faces of α and β tubulin subunits (Zhang et al., 2017), and TOG1-domain containing proteins such as XMAP215 and Stu2, where the TOG1 domain binds predominantly on the β-tubulin face (Byrnes and Slep, 2017), may be less likely to display structural recognition.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the findings for EB1 and Kif5B, supported by citations about binding sites.

claim: EB1 may also preferentially bind to curved protofilaments.
source: As noted above, because outward protofilament curvature at growing microtubule ends is necessarily associated with exposed protofilament edges, we cannot exclude the possibility that EB1 may also preferentially bind to curved protofilaments (Guesdon et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a speculation acknowledging an alternative possibility, with a citation.

claim: Decreased steric hindrance can increase the arrival rate of EB1 to protofilament edges by ~70 fold (~6000%).
source: However, we find that decreased steric hindrance can increase the arrival rate of EB1 to protofilament edges by ~70 fold (~6000%, Figure 3), while no similar effect would apply to protofilament curvature.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the simulation data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Outward protofilament curvature was not routinely observed at holes and defects within the lattice.
source: Further, we did not routinely observe outward protofilament curvature at holes and defects within the lattice (Figure 2B)
evidence: This is an observation from the electron microscopy data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: EB1's dimerization activity would not alter the observed microtubule structural preference in simulations, but would likely increase the dwell time of edge-associated EB1.
source: We anticipate that EB1's dimerization activity would not alter the observed microtubule structural preference in our simulations, but would likely increase the dwell time of edge-associated EB1
evidence: This is a speculation about how EB1 dimerization would affect the simulation results.

claim: A high steric hindrance barrier impedes EB1 from binding directly into the pocket-like interface between four adjacent tubulin dimers in the lattice.
source: In conclusion, we find that a high steric hindrance barrier impedes EB1 from binding directly into the pocket-like interface between four adjacent tubulin dimers in the lattice, and that this barrier is markedly reduced at tapered microtubule ends.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the simulation and experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Protofilament edge-binding greatly increases the arrival rate of EB1 to growing microtubule plus-ends, which facilitates EB1 tip tracking in cells.
source: Protofilament edge-binding greatly increases the arrival rate of EB1 to growing microtubule plus-ends, which facilitates EB1 tip tracking in cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined experimental and simulation data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Microtubule-associated protein binding rates are influenced by the location and conformation of the protein binding interface.
source: Finally, our results support a general principle in which microtubule-associated protein binding rates are influenced by the location and conformation of the protein binding interface.
evidence: This is a general principle derived from the findings presented in the manuscript.
